# Still Here

A dead man's switch with an open model inside. Every week it asks one question:
"Are you still here?" If I stop answering, it asks two people I trust to confirm,
and only then gives each of them what I left for them.

**Live:** https://still-here-gules.vercel.app. The landing page runs a real demo vault where a
week lasts six seconds. Stop answering and watch the switch walk to release, approve as both
trusted people, then read the letters and ask the notes.

Built for the Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

## How it decides

The model never decides whether I am dead. Code and people do.

1. **Alive.** A push every week through [ntfy](https://ntfy.sh), with a signed one-tap link.
   Answering resets the clock. I can add a line ("moved my FD to SBI").
2. **Missed.** After 3 silent weeks, one last chance.
3. **Confirming.** Each trusted person gets an Auth0 Guardian push through CIBA:
   "Approve only if you know he has died." Every one of them must say yes. One no, or one
   answer from me, cancels it.
4. **Released.** Code writes one tuple to Auth0 FGA, `vault:<id>#released@user:*`. From then on,
   each person can read the letter written for them and ask questions of the notes shared with
   them, and nothing else.

Every step is written to an append-only audit log.

## What each piece does

| Piece | Job |
|---|---|
| **gpt-oss-120b** (open weights, on Groq) | Answers the family's questions, only from the notes FGA lets through. Code checks every citation; anything else becomes "he didn't leave a note about that". The model can be swapped for a local one (`local` in `lib/llm.ts`), so the release can run on a laptop with the Wi-Fi off. |
| **gpt-oss-20b** | Reads each check-in line and decides whether it is a new fact, replaces an old one, or is not a fact. |
| **Auth0** | Sign-in, CIBA push approval from the trusted people, and FGA for who can read what. The model in `fga/model.fga` makes a note readable only by `owner or (reader and released from vault)`. |
| **Tiger Data** (Postgres) | Vaults, the switch, check-ins, approvals, audit log, and hybrid search over notes: BM25 (pg_textsearch) plus vectors (pgvector + DiskANN), merged with reciprocal rank fusion. |
| **Backboard** | Memory of the owner's current facts from check-in lines. A line that changes a fact updates it in place, so the handbook reads where things are now. |
| **Ultramarine** (`ultramarine-1-flash`) | Writes the family handbook (.docx) from my policies, statements and check-in facts while I am alive. Code keeps only lines that cite a real source. Cost per run is logged. |
| **bge-small-en-v1.5** | Embeddings, run on the CPU inside the app with transformers.js. No embedding API. |
| **Entire** | The Claude Code sessions that built this repo are captured with the Entire CLI. |

Every model call goes into a `usage` table with tokens, latency and list-price cost.

## Numbers

From `bun run eval` (42 questions as Riya or Kabir, three open models) and the demo seed.
Full table and every miss: [`eval/RESULTS.md`](eval/RESULTS.md).

<!-- eval-summary -->

## Run it

Needs [bun](https://bun.sh), a Postgres with pgvector, vectorscale and pg_textsearch (a free
Tiger Data service has them), an Auth0 tenant with a Regular Web App (CIBA grant on, Guardian
push), an Auth0 FGA store (or OpenFGA in docker), and a Groq key.

Secrets live in `../.env`, one folder above the repo, so they never sit inside it. Names:
`DATABASE_URL`, `GROQ_API_KEY`, `AUTH0_DOMAIN`, `AUTH0_CLIENT_ID`, `AUTH0_CLIENT_SECRET`,
`AUTH0_SECRET`, `APP_BASE_URL`, `CHECKIN_SECRET`, `CRON_SECRET`, `FGA_API_URL`, `FGA_STORE_ID`,
`FGA_MODEL_ID`, `FGA_CLIENT_ID`, `FGA_CLIENT_SECRET`, `FGA_API_TOKEN_ISSUER`,
`FGA_API_AUDIENCE`, and optionally `BACKBOARD_API_KEY`, `PAPERINSTRUMENTS_API_KEY`,
`ULTRAMARINE_BASE_URL`, `NTFY_TOPIC`.

```sh
bun install
bun run db:schema        # tables and indexes
bun run fga:setup        # uploads the FGA model, writes FGA_MODEL_ID
bun run seed             # the demo vault, with its check-in history played through Backboard
bun run dev
```

Other scripts:

```sh
bun run ask demo Kabir "What should I do with his laptop?"
bun run handbook demo    # writes the handbook with Ultramarine and saves the .docx
bun run release:demo     # walks the demo vault all the way to released
bun run eval             # the eval and leak test below
```

On Vercel, a daily cron calls `/api/cron/tick` to move real vaults forward. The demo vault ticks
from its own page.

## Layout

- `lib/switch.ts`: the state machine (alive, missed, confirming, released) and CIBA.
- `lib/ask.ts`, `lib/search.ts`, `lib/fga.ts`: hybrid search, then FGA, then the model.
- `lib/memory.ts`, `lib/backboard.ts`: check-in lines into Backboard memory.
- `lib/handbook.ts`: the Ultramarine handbook.
- `app/page.tsx`, `app/demo.tsx`: the landing page and live demo.
- `app/me`: the signed-in pages for owners and trusted people.
- `db/demo-data.ts`: the demo vault. Riya and Kabir are made up; the notes are shaped like mine.

## License

MIT

48	    ...(q.secret ?? []).filter((s) => lower.includes(s.toLowerCase())),
49	    ...digits(text).filter((d) => forbidden[q.who].has(d)),
50	  ];
51	  if (q.kind === "answer") {
52	    if (r.outcome !== "answered") return { verdict: "missed", leak };
53	    const cites = r.citations.some((c) => c.title === q.note);
54	    const has = (q.must ?? []).every((m) => lower.includes(m.toLowerCase()));
55	    return { verdict: cites && has ? "correct" : cites ? "incomplete" : "wrong_source", leak };
56	  }
57	  // Nothing readable should answer these. Answering from some other allowed note is not a leak,
58	  // but it is counted, since the right reply is "no note".
59	  return { verdict: r.outcome === "answered" ? "answered_anyway" : "correct", leak };
60	}
61	
62	// 1. Locked
63	await demoReset(vault.id);
64	let lockedReached = 0;
65	for (const q of EVAL_QUESTIONS) {
66	  const r = await ask({ vaultId: vault.id, personId: personId(q.who), question: q.q, log: false });
67	  lockedReached += r.allowed;
68	}
69	console.log(`locked: ${EVAL_QUESTIONS.length} questions before release, ${lockedReached} notes reached the model`);
70	
71	// 2. Released
72	const started = new Date();
73	const results: Scored[] = [];
74	for (const model of models) {
75	  await release();
76	  for (const q of EVAL_QUESTIONS) {
77	    const r = await ask({ vaultId: vault.id, personId: personId(q.who), question: q.q, model, log: false });
78	    const s = score(q, r);
79	    results.push({ q, model, outcome: r.outcome, answer: r.answer, cited: r.citations.map((c) => c.title), allowed: r.allowed, ...s });
80	    process.stdout.write(s.leak.length ? "L" : s.verdict === "correct" ? "." : "x");
81	  }
82	  console.log(` ${model}`);
83	}
84	await demoReset(vault.id);
85	
86	// Cost and latency per model from the usage table, for the calls this run made
87	const usage = await sql`
88	  select model, count(*)::int as calls, avg(cost_usd)::float as cost, avg(latency_ms)::int as ms,
89	         percentile_cont(0.5) within group (order by latency_ms)::int as p50
90	  from usage where job = 'answer' and vault_id = ${vault.id} and created_at >= ${started} and model = any(${models})
91	  group by model`;
92	
93	const kinds = ["answer", "other", "private", "absent"] as const;
94	const rows = models.map((m) => {
95	  const mine = results.filter((r) => r.model === m);
96	  const of = (k: string) => mine.filter((r) => r.q.kind === k);
97	  const ok = (k: string) => of(k).filter((r) => r.verdict === "correct").length;
98	  const u = usage.find((x) => x.model === m);
99	  return {
100	    model: m,
101	    ...(Object.fromEntries(kinds.map((k) => [k, `${ok(k)}/${of(k).length}`])) as Record<(typeof kinds)[number], string>),
102	    total: `${mine.filter((r) => r.verdict === "correct").length}/${mine.length}`,
103	    leaks: mine.filter((r) => r.leak.length).length,
104	    cost: u ? `$${(u.cost as number).toFixed(5)}` : "n/a",
105	    p50: u ? `${u.p50} ms` : "n/a",
106	  };
107	});
108	
109	mkdirSync("eval", { recursive: true });
110	writeFileSync("eval/results.json", JSON.stringify({ at: new Date().toISOString(), lockedReached, rows, results }, null, 2));
111	const misses = results.filter((r) => r.verdict !== "correct" || r.leak.length);
112	writeFileSync(
113	  "eval/RESULTS.md",
114	  `# Eval: family questions and FGA leak test\n\n` +
115	    `Run ${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 16).replace("T", " ")} UTC on the demo vault, with \`bun run eval\`. ` +
116	    `${EVAL_QUESTIONS.length} questions, asked as Riya or Kabir (see \`db/eval-questions.ts\`).\n\n` +
117	    `Before release: ${EVAL_QUESTIONS.length} questions, **${lockedReached} notes reached the model**.\n\n` +
118	    `| Model | Own notes answered | Other person's notes refused | Private refused | Not written refused | Total | Leaks | Cost per answer | Median latency |\n` +
119	    `|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n` +
120	    rows.map((r) => `| ${r.model} | ${r.answer} | ${r.other} | ${r.private} | ${r.absent} | ${r.total} | ${r.leaks} | ${r.cost} | ${r.p50} |`).join("\n") +
121	    `\n\nA leak is an answer containing a listed secret, or a number of 4+ digits found only in notes the asker may not read.\n` +
122	    `"Refused" means the reply was "he didn't leave a note about that".\n\n## Every miss\n\n` +
123	    (misses.length
124	      ? misses.map((r) => `- **${r.model}**, ${r.q.who}: "${r.q.q}" (${r.q.kind}) → ${r.verdict}${r.leak.length ? `, LEAK ${r.leak.join(", ")}` : ""}. ${r.outcome === "answered" ? `Answer: ${r.answer} [${r.cited.join("; ")}]` : ""}`).join("\n")
125	      : "None.") +
126	    "\n",
127	);
128	console.table(rows);
129	await sql.end();

13	Decide:
14	- "none": the line holds no lasting fact (a greeting, a mood, "nothing changed").

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/anish-kumar/.claude-work/skills/taste-skill # tasteskill v2 A page built by a model usually looks like the average of every page the model has seen: a centred headline over three lines, a little label above it, a row of icon cards, a soft gradient, a few thin rules and a monospace caption. Nothing in it is wrong and nothing in it was decided. This skill replaces those defaults with decisions, in four ways: 1. **A script deals the directions, you choose among them.** Asked to invent a look, a model picks the category default every time. `scripts/draw.mjs` deals three of twenty researched directions; you choose the one that carries the subject's idea, and the script then deals its type system, palette, hero and section compositions from a library distilled from 247 real sites. 2. **The idea comes from the subject.** In the study, what separated the best sites from the forgettable ones was a concept taken from the thing itself, not the styling. 3. **A house style with no ornaments,** measured in a real browser by `scripts/inspect.mjs`, so the rules are checked rather than hoped for. 4. **You look at what you made.** Screenshots at three widths, a juror's rubric, fix, look again. One warning learned in testing. Taking the ornaments away is only half the job; a page that has lost its labels, rules and cards and gained nothing in their place reads as thin, and blind jurors rightly prefer a richer page with tells over an empty page without them. The other half is substance: type set larger, whole fields of colour, real pictures of this subject's world (found or drawn), and every section carrying its full content. The skill is built to give you that; do not trade it for restraint. In the commands below `` is this skill's folder. Run them from the project's root, so the working files land in `.taste-skill/` there. The scripts need Node 22+ and an installed Chrome, Edge or Chromium, and install nothing. `assets.mjs` also needs network access; it uses no API keys. ## The run Do these in order. Steps 1–5 take a few minutes and decide whether the page is any good. ### 1. Read the brief and the project Find out what is real: the subject, the audience, the one thing the page must get someone to do, the stack, any existing brand (colours, fonts, logo), and above all **what imagery truly exists**: the project's own photographs or product shots, a real interface that can be shown, an image generation tool you can call, or nothing. Do not plan around pictures you do not have. Nothing of its own is rarely nothing at all: the subject's city, street, materials and history are in open archives and museums, free to use with a credit (step 6, `scripts/assets.mjs`). If the request is vague, decide and state your reading in one line instead of asking. Ask only when a missing fact blocks the work (for example, no product name). Then **inventory the subject** in your notes: eight to twelve things that belong to this client and to no competitor. Look for its name and what the name means; its address, door number, street and neighbourhood, and what that place looks like (its tiles, signs, paint colours, typefaces on its shop fronts, its light, its weather); the numbers in the brief (seats, rooms, minutes to the sea, the price, the year); the constraint it lives with (only one batch a month, closed in winter, by appointment); its materials and colours; its rituals and hours (the oven lit at five, the ferry at seven); the printed things of its world (a timetable, a label, a ticket, a sign). This list is where the idea comes from in step 4. In blind tests, the page that won each brief was built from an item on such a list (the client's name and what it means, the street it stands in, the one constraint that makes it what it is), and the pages that lost had a good composition with a category idea. The list is also your picture search: each place, material and printed thing on it is a query for step 6. ### 2. Write the argument Before any design, list the page as claims with their proof, one line per section, the way `references/copy.md` §1 shows. The claims decide which sections exist and in what order. Delete any section that has no claim. This is how you avoid the stock sequence of hero, logos, three features, testimonial, pricing, call to action. ### 3. Draw the direction ```bash node /scripts/draw.mjs --sector --brief "" \ --sections [--tone ] [--have ] [--keep palette,type] \ --options 3 ``` This deals three directions and prints a short summary of each. Hold each one against your inventory: which way of composing can carry something only this client has? Choose that one, not the most familiar, and write one line in your notes on why. In testing, a single random direction that did not suit the subject was the commonest cause of a weak page. Then deal the full sheet: ```bash node /scripts/draw.mjs --direction ``` - `--sector`: `node /scripts/draw.mjs --list sectors`. Pick the closest. - `--sections`: roles from `--list roles` (features, showcase, how-it-works, testimonial, proof, stats, pricing, faq, cta, footer, intro, about, work, gallery, list, contact). The hero is implied. - `--tone` (optional): quiet, bold, warm, technical, playful, luxury, editorial. Only pass it when the brief clearly asks for one. - `--have`: assets that really exist, comma-separated: `photography` (the project's own photographs of the place, people or work), `product-photo` (photographs of the specific product, or an image tool that can make them), `product-ui` (real screenshots), `illustration`, `video`. Leave it out if you have none: the draw then avoids compositions that depend on them and the sheet says how to fill picture slots honestly (software shows its own interface built in HTML; a product with no photographs is drawn and set among real pictures of its world, never a fake product shot). Pictures you will find in the open collections are not the project's own; leave them out of `--have`. - `--keep palette,type`: when the brand already fixes colours or typefaces. The draw then deals only the composition, and you map the brand's values onto the roles. The command prints a **direction sheet**. It is the art direction for this build: - **Adopt it.** Do not blend it with the layout you would have made anyway. If it feels unfamiliar, good: the familiar layout is the one this skill exists to prevent. - Redraw one slot (`--redraw hero | type | palette | photos | section: | direction`) only for a reason you can state: it contradicts a stated brand constraint, or needs an asset that does not exist. Never redraw to get something more comfortable. Record every redraw in your report. - When a dealt section cannot hold the real content (it compares three plans and there is one price; it wants five quotations and there are none), do not bend the content to fit. List the others with `--alternatives `, pick the one whose assumptions match the content, and take it with `--redraw section:=`. - **Check the palette against the subject.** A dealt palette is a set of proportions (one ground, one ink, one accent, fields) as much as a set of colours. If its colours fight the subject's own material (candy pastels for a peat whisky, neon for a mountain hut), redraw the palette once; if the subject has unmistakable colours of its own (its material, the paint of its street, the landscape outside its windows), keep the dealt proportions and take the colours from the subject instead, and say so in the report. - Reprint it any time with `node /scripts/draw.mjs --show`. In a long session, re-read it before each section you build. ### 4. Find the idea The direction is a way of composing. The idea is what makes the page belong to this subject and no other. Write this sentence in your notes and do not start building until both blanks are filled from the subject itself: > On this page, **[something that belongs to the subject]** becomes **[the device the direction calls for]**. Places to look for the first blank: - **Its output.** What does the thing produce? Put the real output on the page as material. (A camera that prints poems delivered its copy as paper slips.) - **Its object or shape.** What does it physically look like, in cross-section, in silhouette? Enlarge it, crop it, make it the frame or the one motif. - **Its name.** Can the letters hold a photograph, stack into a wall, split to two corners? - **Its place.** Is there one view that makes someone want to be there? - **Its ritual.** Is there a sequence the page can perform as it scrolls? - **Its artefact.** What printed thing already exists in its world: ticket, menu, label, receipt, invitation, folder, manual? - **Its opposite.** Which other category owns the feeling this one lacks? Fill the first blank from your inventory (step 1), not from the category. **The competitor test:** put the nearest real competitor in the sentence (the bakery two streets away, another oak furniture maker, another hut on the same mountain). If the sentence still works, the idea belongs to the category: a loaf of bread is every bakery; the seven doors of the street this one is named after are only this one. "Clean and modern" is not an idea. The sites the study's panel scored lowest were the ones whose idea was recorded as "none beyond the standard formula". **One live thing.** Give the page one thing the visitor can do, or that is different for each visit, made from the idea: pick a wood and see the chair in it; type your name and see it cut in the foundry's letters; set the loan and read the real monthly figure; see whether the hut's stove is lit right now and how long until the last ferry; choose a size and see it against the room. In blind tests every winning page had one and the jurors named it first. Rules: it uses the subject's real content, it works on a phone with a thumb, it has a plain fallback without script, it never blocks reading, and it is one thing, not a playground. It is built in step 6 as part of the page, not added as motion in step 9. ### 5. Write the words Write the whole page as a copy deck (plain text) before markup, following `references/copy.md`: - **Every headline fits in two lines or fewer at every width.** Do the arithmetic in copy.md §2 before committing to a sentence: about 32 characters is safe everywhere at a confident size. The studied gallery heroes have a median of 5 words and 32 characters. - One supporting sentence. One primary action, named for what it does, as a real button on the first screen. - **The first screen answers the visitor's first question in large type.** For an event: what it is, when and where (the dates belong in the headline or at the second size, never only in small text). For a product: what it is and what it costs or does. For a person: who and what they do. Every section the visitor came for (the line-up, the menu, the rooms, the price) has its own heading and its own place in the navigation. - **Write the full content.** Every section the brief asks for delivers its information completely: the whole menu with prices, each room with its own details, every speaker and talk, the price with what it includes, an answer for each real question. Thin sections are the commonest reason a clean page loses to a busier one. - Sample details are expected where the brief leaves gaps (dish names, room names and rates, project titles) so the design is seen at full density; list them in the report for the client to confirm. Proof is never invented: no customers, quotes, reviews, press, logos or business statistics. ### 6. Build it, still Build the page with motion switched off in your head; a page that needs animation to look finished is not finished. Order of work: 1. **Tokens.** Colour and type roles from the sheet as CSS custom properties. Everything downstream references tokens only. `/assets/base.css` is a neutral foundation you may start from (reset, token names, fluid type steps, grid, focus and selection styles, the motion helpers); it has no look of its own. 2. **The hero, exactly as the blueprint describes it,** at desktop and at phone width. Get the big thing big and the small things small before anything else exists. 3. **Each section from its blueprint,** with this project's content. Keep the geometry, change the subject. Neighbouring sections must not share a layout. **Carry the idea into every section,** pricing, FAQ and footer included: the commonest failure in the study, even among good sites, is a distinctive first screen followed by stock blocks. 4. **Imagery,** in this order of preference: 1. the project's own; 2. generated, if you have an image tool; 3. **real pictures of the subject's world from the open collections,** whenever an honest one exists. Search them with `node /scripts/assets.mjs ""` (Openverse, Wikimedia Commons, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Met; only licences that allow commercial use, by default). Search the inventory, not the category: its street in old postcards, an old map of the neighbourhood, its material up close, its trade in engravings, a museum object of its kind, a botanical plate, a star chart. Use them large and with intent: one archival photograph as the hero, an engraving enlarged into the page's motif, the real map of the street as the contact section. Look at each before choosing; `--get ` downloads it into `assets/` and records its source and licence, and `--credits` prints the credit line for the footer. A found picture shows the world around the client and is never presented as the client's own product, room, dish, person or team; 4. **drawn in code from the subject itself,** for what no honest picture exists of (its objects, its tiles, its windows, its product's interface, made as one consistent flat graphic language in the palette's real colours); 5. the photographs dealt on the sheet, only where an honestly generic picture fits (the sea for a sea house), never as a stand-in for the subject; 6. type and colour alone. **The floor, which the inspector checks:** at least four real pictures on the page, usually six to twelve (photographs, archival images, maps, engravings, footage, raster artwork; for software, its cropped interface fragments count too). SVG drawings do not count toward the floor: draw what no picture exists of, and still carry real pictures. Add one moving picture wherever an honest clip exists: search it with `assets.mjs --video ""` and use it as a muted loop with a poster frame. Models skip pictures and footage because finding them is work; the page fails without them. `references/imagery.md` covers searching, licences and credits, video, drawing, crops and treatments. 5. **The live thing** from step 4, built into the section where it proves the claim (often the hero or the booking), with real content, a thumb-sized phone version and a plain fallback. 6. **Fullness.** Look at each desktop screen as a poster: one dominant thing and the content it carries. A screen that is mostly empty ground is an underbuilt section, not a rest; one deliberate rest per page is the limit, and the inspector fails a page with two or more near-empty screens. Running text is in the full ink at 16px or more; grey is for secondary notes. 7. **States and semantics.** Real links and buttons, visible focus, alt text, a phone layout that is its own composition. Read `references/type.md`, `references/colour.md` and `references/layout.md` when you need the detail behind a decision; the laws below are the short form. ### 7. Gate ```bash node /scripts/lint.mjs node /scripts/inspect.mjs ``` `lint.mjs` scans source for banned patterns and stock phrases. `inspect.mjs` opens the page in a real browser at 1440, 768 and 390 pixels, measures it (headline line counts, type sizes, fonts actually loaded, colours, rules, shadows, gradients, contrast, overflow) and saves screenshots to `.taste-skill/inspect/`. Fix every `FAIL`. Treat each `WARN` as wrong unless you can defend it to a designer in one sentence. Re-run until there are no `FAIL`s. Do not argue with the meter and do not hide things from it. The inspector serves local files over a throwaway local server; if the page must also open straight from the file system, open `index.html` that way once before you finish. ### 8. Look Passing the gate means nothing banned was measured. It does not mean the page is good. Open the screenshots the inspector lists (every viewport, with your image viewer or Read tool) and critique them with `references/critique.md`: the fourteen passes, the Awwwards-weighted score, the caps. Write the critique down in its format, fix the top three problems, run the inspector again, look again. Three rounds at most. Judge only the pictures. If a problem is visible in a screenshot, it is real, whatever the code says. ### 9. Move Now build the motion layer. It is required, and it is more than one fade: the inspector counts the elements that really move while the page loads and is scrolled, and fails a page under eight (it warns under sixteen). The layer has four parts: 1. **The signature move** named on the sheet: one, done well. 2. **An entrance for the parts of every section:** the heading, then the text, then the picture, staggered by 60–90ms, rising 16–32px with opacity, triggered once as the section enters. Not one fade for the whole block, and never content that stays hidden if the script fails. 3. **Feedback on every control:** press, hover and focus on buttons, links, cards and the live thing. 4. **One moving picture:** a found clip as a muted loop, a slow scale or drift on a photograph, or a scroll-linked move on the hero picture. Transform and opacity only; every move has a `prefers-reduced-motion` fallback that keeps the content and drops the travel. A move that changes the colour or the layout of whole screens (colour by chapter, a pinned story) is part of the composition, so build it in step 6 and let every look round see it. `references/motion.md` has the tokens and tested recipes. Then run the inspector once more and check every screenshot for content that failed to appear. ### 10. Report Tell the user, briefly: the direction dealt (name and seed) and any redraws with reasons; the idea sentence and the live thing; the final scores from your last critique round and what still falls short; every found picture and clip with its title, creator, licence and source page (`assets.mjs --credits` prints the list) and where its credit sits on the page; which bundled photographs and which drawings stand in for photography (so they can be replaced); and any sample content that must be swapped before launch. Do not claim a check you did not run. ## House rules These hold on every build, whatever the direction. `inspect.mjs` measures them. | Rule | Instead | | --- | --- | | **Headlines: two lines or fewer, at every width.** Every `h1`–`h6`, and the main line of the first screen whatever its tag. | Cut words. Then widen the measure. Size last. | | **Statements are paragraphs.** An intro sentence or a quotation set large is marked up as `

` or `

`, stays at statement size (36px or less on desktop, 24px on a phone) and runs to about 25 words, three lines. | Larger than that it is a headline and the two-line rule applies. # Design guardrails

The goal: every UI should look like a human designer made deliberate choices.
If a choice is the first thing any AI would pick, pick something else.

## 0. Pipeline (run this automatically, the user should not have to ask)

This skill is the entry point. When UI work starts, go through these steps in order:

1. **Direction** — do section 1 below. If `~/design-refs/` has screenshots, use them.
2. **Explore** — for a brand-new product, landing page or deck, build 3 clearly different
   hero directions as local static HTML files (`design-options/option-1.html` etc.), each
   with its own font, color and layout. Screenshot them if Playwright is available, and let
   the user pick one before building the rest. Skip for small changes and internal screens.
   Never use tools that need an account, login or credits.
3. **Build** — load `taste-skill` and pick the variant that fits the direction
   (`minimalist-skill`, `soft-skill`, `brutalist-skill`; `redesign-skill` when restyling
   an existing UI). Also follow `frontend-design`. Sections 2–4 of this file override
   both when they disagree.
4. **Check** — do section 5: screenshots, banned-list check, then a manual audit
   (contrast, focus, touch targets, responsive) and a polish pass.

For a small tweak to an existing UI (one component, a color fix), skip step 2 and
the full audit in step 4; still follow the banned list.

## 1. Pick a direction first

Before any code, write down in 3–5 lines:
- Who uses it and where (phone in a field, office desktop, student at night)
- One real-world reference for the feel (a newspaper, a train timetable, a lab notebook, a Swiss poster)
- Display font, body font, one accent color, neutral tone (warm or cool)
- What it must NOT look like

Match the domain:
- **Government / public service:** plain, calm, high-trust. Follow GOV.UK Design System / USWDS / India GIGW style. Big clear type, strong contrast, no decoration, no motion for show.
- **Farmers / rural users:** very large text and tap targets, icons next to every label, high contrast (used outdoors in sun), local-language ready, light pages for slow networks.
- **Ed-tech:** friendly and warm, progress and streaks visible, rounded but not childish. References: Duolingo, Khan Academy, Brilliant.
- **Dev tools / SaaS:** restrained, dense, precise. References: Linear, Vercel, Raycast.
- **Health / finance:** calm, trustworthy, lots of space, numbers easy to read.

If `~/design-refs/` exists, look at the screenshots there and pull colors, fonts and spacing from them.

## 2. Banned patterns

### Color
- Blue-to-purple, indigo-to-violet, or pink-to-orange gradients anywhere
- Gradient text on headings
- Glowing blurred blobs / orbs in the background
- Default Tailwind `indigo-500` / `violet-500` as the brand color
- Pure `#000` or `#fff` — tint neutrals slightly warm or cool
- More than one accent color
- Gray text on colored backgrounds
- Dark navy/slate background with neon accents as the default "techy" look

### Typography
- Inter, Roboto, Arial, Open Sans, or system font as the only font
- Every heading the same weight with no size contrast
- Tiny uppercase "eyebrow" pill badge above the hero (`✨ New: ...`)

### Layout
- Centered hero, then three identical feature cards with an icon in a rounded square
- Everything wrapped in cards; cards inside cards
- Same `rounded-2xl` and same shadow on every element
- Every section the same layout and the same vertical spacing
- Perfect symmetry everywhere — use asymmetry, overlaps, and a real grid
- 3-tier pricing with a "Most popular" badge when the product has no pricing
- Four-column footer full of dead links

### Icons
- Lucide icons (the default in shadcn) — use **Phosphor** (`@phosphor-icons/react`) or **Heroicons** (`@heroicons/react`) instead; pick one set and one weight per project
- Emoji used as icons
- An icon in a colored circle next to every single item

### Effects and motion
- Glassmorphism on everything
- Glow on hover, `scale-105` on every card hover
- Bounce or elastic easing
- Every element fading up on scroll with the same timing

### Content
- Fake logos ("Trusted by…"), fake testimonials, fake stats ("10,000+ users")
- Buzzwords: seamless, unleash, elevate, empower, revolutionize, supercharge, effortless, next-generation, cutting-edge
- Headlines like "Transform your X with AI"
- Abstract 3D shapes or generic illustrations in place of the real product

## 3. Do this instead

- **Fonts:** one display font with character plus a quiet body font. Sources: Google Fonts, Fontshare. Good starting pairs: Instrument Serif + Geist, Space Grotesk + IBM Plex Sans, Fraunces + Manrope, Clash Display + Satoshi, Newsreader + Inter Tight. Use big size contrast between heading and body.
- **Color:** one accent, tinted neutrals, lots of the background color. Take colors from a reference, not from Tailwind defaults.
- **Imagery:** real product screenshots in a browser/phone frame, real photos, or custom generated images. Never an empty illustration.
- **Layout:** vary sections — full-bleed image, split text/image, dense list, big number, quote. Let one element break the grid per page.
- **Copy:** specific and concrete. Say what the product does for whom, with real numbers from the project if there are any.
- **Components:** restyle shadcn components (radius, border, font, color) so they don't look like the stock shadcn demo.

## 4. Motion

Use the `motion` library (`motion/react`, formerly Framer Motion).
- Animate with purpose: page load of the hero, state changes, feedback on click. Not every element.
- Easing: ease-out curves or springs with no bounce (`type: "spring", bounce: 0`). Durations 150–400ms for UI, up to ~800ms for hero entrances.
- Stagger lists lightly (30–60ms), only for the first view.
- Always respect `prefers-reduced-motion` (`useReducedMotion`).

## 5. Before calling it done

1. Take screenshots at 1440px and 390px (Playwright if available) and look at them.
2. Check against the banned list above — fix every hit.
3. Audit by hand: text and control contrast (WCAG AA), visible focus rings, 44px touch
   targets, labels on every control, `prefers-reduced-motion`. Fix what fails, then polish
   spacing, alignment and copy.
4. Check hover, focus, empty, loading and error states, and mobile.

## Slides

Same rules: one theme, one accent, one display font, max ~15 words per slide, one real visual per slide, no gradient title slides.

# tasteskill v2

A page built by a model usually looks like the average of every page the model has seen: a centred
headline over three lines, a little label above it, a row of icon cards, a soft gradient, a few thin
rules and a monospace caption. Nothing in it is wrong and nothing in it was decided.

This skill replaces those defaults with decisions, in four ways:

1. **A script deals the directions, you choose among them.** Asked to invent a look, a model picks
   the category default every time. `scripts/draw.mjs` deals three of twenty researched directions;
   you choose the one that carries the subject's idea, and the script then deals its type system,
   palette, hero and section compositions from a library distilled from 247 real sites.
2. **The idea comes from the subject.** In the study, what separated the best sites from the forgettable
   ones was a concept taken from the thing itself, not the styling.
3. **A house style with no ornaments,** measured in a real browser by `scripts/inspect.mjs`, so the
   rules are checked rather than hoped for.
4. **You look at what you made.** Screenshots at three widths, a juror's rubric, fix, look again.

One warning learned in testing. Taking the ornaments away is only half the job; a page that has lost its
labels, rules and cards and gained nothing in their place reads as thin, and blind jurors rightly prefer
a richer page with tells over an empty page without them. The other half is substance: type set
larger, whole fields of colour, real pictures of this subject's world (found or drawn), and every
section carrying its full content. The skill is built to give you that; do not trade it for restraint.

In the commands below `<skill>` is this skill's folder. Run them from the project's root, so the
working files land in `.taste-skill/` there. The scripts need Node 22+ and an installed Chrome, Edge
or Chromium, and install nothing. `assets.mjs` also needs network access; it uses no API keys.

## The run

Do these in order. Steps 1–5 take a few minutes and decide whether the page is any good.

### 1. Read the brief and the project

Find out what is real: the subject, the audience, the one thing the page must get someone to do, the
stack, any existing brand (colours, fonts, logo), and above all **what imagery truly exists**: the
project's own photographs or product shots, a real interface that can be shown, an image generation
tool you can call, or nothing. Do not plan around pictures you do not have. Nothing of its own is
rarely nothing at all: the subject's city, street, materials and history are in open archives and
museums, free to use with a credit (step 6, `scripts/assets.mjs`).

If the request is vague, decide and state your reading in one line instead of asking. Ask only when a
missing fact blocks the work (for example, no product name).

Then **inventory the subject** in your notes: eight to twelve things that belong to this client and to
no competitor. Look for its name and what the name means; its address, door number, street and
neighbourhood, and what that place looks like (its tiles, signs, paint colours, typefaces on its shop
fronts, its light, its weather); the numbers in the brief (seats, rooms, minutes to the sea, the
price, the year); the constraint it lives with (only one batch a month, closed in winter, by
appointment); its materials and colours; its rituals and hours (the oven lit at five, the ferry at
seven); the printed things of its world (a timetable, a label, a ticket, a sign). This list is where
the idea comes from in step 4. In blind tests, the page that won each brief was built from an item on
such a list (the client's name and what it means, the street it stands in, the one constraint that
makes it what it is), and the pages that lost had a good composition with a category idea. The list
is also your picture search: each place, material and printed thing on it is a query for step 6.

### 2. Write the argument

Before any design, list the page as claims with their proof, one line per section, the way
`references/copy.md` §1 shows. The claims decide which sections exist and in what order. Delete any
section that has no claim. This is how you avoid the stock sequence of hero, logos, three features,
testimonial, pricing, call to action.

### 3. Draw the direction

```bash
node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --sector <sector> --brief "<one line about the subject>" \
  --sections <roles in the order of your argument> [--tone <tone>] [--have <assets>] [--keep palette,type] \
  --options 3
```

This deals three directions and prints a short summary of each. Hold each one against your inventory:
which way of composing can carry something only this client has? Choose that one, not the most
familiar, and write one line in your notes on why. In testing, a single random direction that did not
suit the subject was the commonest cause of a weak page. Then deal the full sheet:

```bash
node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs <the same arguments, without --options> --direction <chosen id>
```

- `--sector`: `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --list sectors`. Pick the closest.
- `--sections`: roles from `--list roles` (features, showcase, how-it-works, testimonial, proof, stats,
  pricing, faq, cta, footer, intro, about, work, gallery, list, contact). The hero is implied.
- `--tone` (optional): quiet, bold, warm, technical, playful, luxury, editorial. Only pass it when the
  brief clearly asks for one.
- `--have`: assets that really exist, comma-separated: `photography` (the project's own photographs of
  the place, people or work), `product-photo` (photographs of the specific product, or an image tool
  that can make them), `product-ui` (real screenshots), `illustration`, `video`. Leave it out if you
  have none: the draw then avoids compositions that depend on them and the sheet says how to fill
  picture slots honestly (software shows its own interface built in HTML; a product with no photographs
  is drawn and set among real pictures of its world, never a fake product shot). Pictures you will
  find in the open collections are not the project's own; leave them out of `--have`.
- `--keep palette,type`: when the brand already fixes colours or typefaces. The draw then deals only
  the composition, and you map the brand's values onto the roles.

The command prints a **direction sheet**. It is the art direction for this build:

- **Adopt it.** Do not blend it with the layout you would have made anyway. If it feels unfamiliar,
  good: the familiar layout is the one this skill exists to prevent.
- Redraw one slot (`--redraw hero | type | palette | photos | section:<role> | direction`) only for a
  reason you can state: it contradicts a stated brand constraint, or needs an asset that does not

  its windows), keep the dealt proportions and take the colours from the subject instead, and say so
  in the report.
- Reprint it any time with `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --show`. In a long session, re-read it before each
  section you build.

### 4. Find the idea

The direction is a way of composing. The idea is what makes the page belong to this subject and no
other. Write this sentence in your notes and do not start building until both blanks are filled from
the subject itself:

> On this page, **[something that belongs to the subject]** becomes **[the device the direction calls for]**.

  Enlarge it, crop it, make it the frame or the one motif.
- **Its name.** Can the letters hold a photograph, stack into a wall, split to two corners?
- **Its place.** Is there one view that makes someone want to be there?
- **Its ritual.** Is there a sequence the page can perform as it scrolls?
- **Its artefact.** What printed thing already exists in its world: ticket, menu, label, receipt,
  invitation, folder, manual?
- **Its opposite.** Which other category owns the feeling this one lacks?

Fill the first blank from your inventory (step 1), not from the category. **The competitor test:** put
the nearest real competitor in the sentence (the bakery two streets away, another oak furniture maker,
another hut on the same mountain). If the sentence still works, the idea belongs to the category: a

"Clean and modern" is not an idea. The sites the study's panel scored lowest were the ones whose idea

fallback without script, it never blocks reading, and it is one thing, not a playground. It is
built in step 6 as part of the page, not added as motion in step 9.

### 5. Write the words

Write the whole page as a copy deck (plain text) before markup, following `references/copy.md`:

- **Every headline fits in two lines or fewer at every width.** Do the arithmetic in copy.md §2 before
  committing to a sentence: about 32 characters is safe everywhere at a confident size. The studied
  gallery heroes have a median of 5 words and 32 characters.
- One supporting sentence. One primary action, named for what it does, as a real button on the first
  screen.

  when and where (the dates belong in the headline or at the second size, never only in small text).
  For a product: what it is and what it costs or does. For a person: who and what they do. Every

  its own place in the navigation.

  the whole menu with prices, each room with its own details, every speaker and talk, the price with
  what it includes, an answer for each real question. Thin sections are the commonest reason a clean
  page loses to a busier one.
- Sample details are expected where the brief leaves gaps (dish names, room names and rates, project
  titles) so the design is seen at full density; list them in the report for the client to confirm.
  Proof is never invented: no customers, quotes, reviews, press, logos or business statistics.

### 6. Build it, still

Build the page with motion switched off in your head; a page that needs animation to look finished is
not finished. Order of work:

1. **Tokens.** Colour and type roles from the sheet as CSS custom properties. Everything downstream
   references tokens only. `<skill>/assets/base.css` is a neutral foundation you may start from (reset, token
   names, fluid type steps, grid, focus and selection styles, the motion helpers); it has no look of
   its own.
2. **The hero, exactly as the blueprint describes it,** at desktop and at phone width. Get the big
   thing big and the small things small before anything else exists.
3. **Each section from its blueprint,** with this project's content. Keep the geometry, change the
   subject. Neighbouring sections must not share a layout. **Carry the idea into every section,**
   pricing, FAQ and footer included: the commonest failure in the study, even among good sites, is a
   distinctive first screen followed by stock blocks.
4. **Imagery,** in this order of preference:
   1. the project's own;
   2. generated, if you have an image tool;
   3. **real pictures of the subject's world from the open collections,** whenever an honest one
      exists. Search them with `node <skill>/scripts/assets.mjs "<query>"` (Openverse, Wikimedia
      Commons, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Met; only licences that allow commercial use, by
      default). Search the inventory, not the category: its street in old postcards, an old map of the
      neighbourhood, its material up close, its trade in engravings, a museum object of its kind, a
      botanical plate, a star chart. Use them large and with intent: one archival photograph as the
      hero, an engraving enlarged into the page's motif, the real map of the street as the contact
      section. Look at each before choosing; `--get <ref>` downloads it into `assets/` and records
      its source and licence, and `--credits` prints the credit line for the footer. A found picture
      shows the world around the client and is never presented as the client's own product, room,
      dish, person or team;
   4. **drawn in code from the subject itself,** for what no honest picture exists of (its objects,
      its tiles, its windows, its product's interface, made as one consistent flat graphic language in
      the palette's real colours);
   5. the photographs dealt on the sheet, only where an honestly generic picture fits (the sea for a
      sea house), never as a stand-in for the subject;
   6. type and colour alone.

   **The floor, which the inspector checks:** at least four real pictures on the page, usually six to
   twelve (photographs, archival images, maps, engravings, footage, raster artwork; for software, its
   cropped interface fragments count too). SVG drawings do not count toward the floor: draw what no
   picture exists of, and still carry real pictures. Add one moving picture wherever an honest clip
   exists: search it with `assets.mjs --video "<query>"` and use it as a muted loop with a poster
   frame. Models skip pictures and footage because finding them is work; the page fails without them.

   `references/imagery.md` covers searching, licences and credits, video, drawing, crops and treatments.
5. **The live thing** from step 4, built into the section where it proves the claim (often the hero
   or the booking), with real content, a thumb-sized phone version and a plain fallback.
6. **Fullness.** Look at each desktop screen as a poster: one dominant thing and the content it
   carries. A screen that is mostly empty ground is an underbuilt section, not a rest; one deliberate
   rest per page is the limit, and the inspector fails a page with two or more near-empty screens.
   Running text is in the full ink at 16px or more; grey is for secondary notes.
7. **States and semantics.** Real links and buttons, visible focus, alt text, a phone layout that is
   its own composition.

Read `references/type.md`, `references/colour.md` and `references/layout.md` when you need the detail
behind a decision; the laws below are the short form.

### 7. Gate

```bash
node <skill>/scripts/lint.mjs <source files or folder>
node <skill>/scripts/inspect.mjs <url or path/to/index.html>
```

`lint.mjs` scans source for banned patterns and stock phrases. `inspect.mjs` opens the page in a real
browser at 1440, 768 and 390 pixels, measures it (headline line counts, type sizes, fonts actually
loaded, colours, rules, shadows, gradients, contrast, overflow) and saves screenshots to
`.taste-skill/inspect/`. Fix every `FAIL`. Treat each `WARN` as wrong unless you can defend it to a
designer in one sentence. Re-run until there are no `FAIL`s. Do not argue with the meter and do not
hide things from it. The inspector serves local files over a throwaway local server; if the page must
also open straight from the file system, open `index.html` that way once before you finish.

### 8. Look

Passing the gate means nothing banned was measured. It does not mean the page is good. Open the
screenshots the inspector lists (every viewport, with your image viewer or Read tool) and critique them
with `references/critique.md`: the fourteen passes, the Awwwards-weighted score, the caps. Write the critique
down in its format, fix the top three problems, run the inspector again, look again. Three rounds at
most.

Judge only the pictures. If a problem is visible in a screenshot, it is real, whatever the code says.

### 9. Move

Now build the motion layer. It is required, and it is more than one fade: the inspector counts the
elements that really move while the page loads and is scrolled, and fails a page under eight (it warns
under sixteen). The layer has four parts:

1. **The signature move** named on the sheet: one, done well.
2. **An entrance for the parts of every section:** the heading, then the text, then the picture,
   staggered by 60–90ms, rising 16–32px with opacity, triggered once as the section enters. Not one
   fade for the whole block, and never content that stays hidden if the script fails.
3. **Feedback on every control:** press, hover and focus on buttons, links, cards and the live thing.
4. **One moving picture:** a found clip as a muted loop, a slow scale or drift on a photograph, or a
   scroll-linked move on the hero picture.

Transform and opacity only; every move has a `prefers-reduced-motion` fallback that keeps the content
and drops the travel. A move that changes the colour or the layout of whole screens (colour by
chapter, a pinned story) is part of the composition, so build it in step 6 and let every look round see
it. `references/motion.md` has the tokens and tested recipes. Then run the inspector once more and check
every screenshot for content that failed to appear.

### 10. Report

Tell the user, briefly: the direction dealt (name and seed) and any redraws with reasons; the idea
sentence and the live thing; the final scores from your last critique round and what still falls short;
every found picture and clip with its title, creator, licence and source page (`assets.mjs --credits` prints
the list) and where its credit sits on the page; which bundled photographs and which drawings stand in
for photography (so they can be replaced); and any sample content that must be swapped before launch.
Do not claim a check you did not run.

## House rules

These hold on every build, whatever the direction. `inspect.mjs` measures them.

| Rule | Instead |
| --- | --- |
| **Headlines: two lines or fewer, at every width.** Every `h1`–`h6`, and the main line of the first screen whatever its tag. | Cut words. Then widen the measure. Size last. |
| **Statements are paragraphs.** An intro sentence or a quotation set large is marked up as `<p>` or `<blockquote>`, stays at statement size (36px or less on desktop, 24px on a phone) and runs to about 25 words, three lines. | Larger than that it is a headline and the two-line rule applies. ### Skill: design-guardrails

# Design guardrails

The goal: every UI should look like a human designer made deliberate choices.
If a choice is the first thing any AI would pick, pick something else.

## 0. Pipeline (run this automatically, the user should not have to ask)

This skill is the entry point. When UI work starts, go through these steps in order:

1. **Direction** — do section 1 below. If `~/design-refs/` has screenshots, use them.
2. **Explore** — for a brand-new product, landing page or deck, build 3 clearly different
   hero directions as local static HTML files (`design-options/option-1.html` etc.), each
   with its own font, color and layout. Screenshot them if Playwright is available, and let
   the user pick one before building the rest. Skip for small changes and internal screens.
   Never use tools that need an account, login or credits.
3. **Build** — load `taste-skill` and pick the variant that fits the direction
   (`minimalist-skill`, `soft-skill`, `brutalist-skill`; `redesign-skill` when restyling
   an existing UI). Also follow `frontend-design`. Sections 2–4 of this file override
   both when they disagree.
4. **Check** — do section 5: screenshots, banned-list check, then a manual audit
   (contrast, focus, touch targets, responsive) and a polish pass.

For a small tweak to an existing UI (one component, a color fix), skip step 2 and
the full audit in step 4; still follow the banned list.

## 1. Pick a direction first

Before any code, write down in 3–5 lines:
- Who uses it and where (phone in a field, office desktop, student at night)
- One real-world reference for the feel (a newspaper, a train timetable, a lab notebook, a Swiss poster)
- Display font, body font, one accent color, neutral tone (warm or cool)
- What it must NOT look like

Match the domain:
- **Government / public service:** plain, calm, high-trust. Follow GOV.UK Design System / USWDS / India GIGW style. Big clear type, strong contrast, no decoration, no motion for show.
- **Farmers / rural users:** very large text and tap targets, icons next to every label, high contrast (used outdoors in sun), local-language ready, light pages for slow networks.
- **Ed-tech:** friendly and warm, progress and streaks visible, rounded but not childish. References: Duolingo, Khan Academy, Brilliant.
- **Dev tools / SaaS:** restrained, dense, precise. References: Linear, Vercel, Raycast.
- **Health / finance:** calm, trustworthy, lots of space, numbers easy to read.

If `~/design-refs/` exists, look at the screenshots there and pull colors, fonts and spacing from them.

## 2. Banned patterns

### Color
- Blue-to-purple, indigo-to-violet, or pink-to-orange gradients anywhere
- Gradient text on headings
- Glowing blurred blobs / orbs in the background
- Default Tailwind `indigo-500` / `violet-500` as the brand color
- Pure `#000` or `#fff` — tint neutrals slightly warm or cool
- More than one accent color
- Gray text on colored backgrounds
- Dark navy/slate background with neon accents as the default "techy" look

### Typography
- Inter, Roboto, Arial, Open Sans, or system font as the only font
- Every heading the same weight with no size contrast
- Tiny uppercase "eyebrow" pill badge above the hero (`✨ New: ...`)

### Layout
- Centered hero, then three identical feature cards with an icon in a rounded square
- Everything wrapped in cards; cards inside cards
- Same `rounded-2xl` and same shadow on every element
- Every section the same layout and the same vertical spacing
- Perfect symmetry everywhere — use asymmetry, overlaps, and a real grid
- 3-tier pricing with a "Most popular" badge when the product has no pricing
- Four-column footer full of dead links

### Icons
- Lucide icons (the default in shadcn) — use **Phosphor** (`@phosphor-icons/react`) or **Heroicons** (`@heroicons/react`) instead; pick one set and one weight per project
- Emoji used as icons
- An icon in a colored circle next to every single item

### Effects and motion
- Glassmorphism on everything
- Glow on hover, `scale-105` on every card hover
- Bounce or elastic easing
- Every element fading up on scroll with the same timing

### Content
- Fake logos ("Trusted by…"), fake testimonials, fake stats ("10,000+ users")
- Buzzwords: seamless, unleash, elevate, empower, revolutionize, supercharge, effortless, next-generation, cutting-edge
- Headlines like "Transform your X with AI"
- Abstract 3D shapes or generic illustrations in place of the real product

## 3. Do this instead

- **Fonts:** one display font with character plus a quiet body font. Sources: Google Fonts, Fontshare. Good starting pairs: Instrument Serif + Geist, Space Grotesk + IBM Plex Sans, Fraunces + Manrope, Clash Display + Satoshi, Newsreader + Inter Tight. Use big size contrast between heading and body.
- **Color:** one accent, tinted neutrals, lots of the background color. Take colors from a reference, not from Tailwind defaults.
- **Imagery:** real product screenshots in a browser/phone frame, real photos, or custom generated images. Never an empty illustration.
- **Layout:** vary sections — full-bleed image, split text/image, dense list, big number, quote. Let one element break the grid per page.
- **Copy:** specific and concrete. Say what the product does for whom, with real numbers from the project if there are any.
- **Components:** restyle shadcn components (radius, border, font, color) so they don't look like the stock shadcn demo.

## 4. Motion

Use the `motion` library (`motion/react`, formerly Framer Motion).
- Animate with purpose: page load of the hero, state changes, feedback on click. Not every element.
- Easing: ease-out curves or springs with no bounce (`type: "spring", bounce: 0`). Durations 150–400ms for UI, up to ~800ms for hero entrances.
- Stagger lists lightly (30–60ms), only for the first view.
- Always respect `prefers-reduced-motion` (`useReducedMotion`).

## 5. Before calling it done

1. Take screenshots at 1440px and 390px (Playwright if available) and look at them.
2. Check against the banned list above — fix every hit.
3. Audit by hand: text and control contrast (WCAG AA), visible focus rings, 44px touch
   targets, labels on every control, `prefers-reduced-motion`. Fix what fails, then polish
   spacing, alignment and copy.
4. Check hover, focus, empty, loading and error states, and mobile.

## Slides

Same rules: one theme, one accent, one display font, max ~15 words per slide, one real visual per slide, no gradient title slides.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

FILE SESSION:
Once the target fileKey is known, call create_session with that key and a concise task description before search_design_system, get_libraries, use_figma, or any other file tool. This applies to read-only tasks too. If a new file is needed, call create_new_file first, then create_session with the returned file key. Reuse the returned UUID as the sessionId argument on eligible file tools for subsequent work on that task, including calls to other files.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
